title: Hubble Snaps a 13-Billion-Year-Old Fireworks Show for July 4th!
summary: Happy 250th birthday, America! To celebrate, NASA's Hubble Space Telescope just sent us a dazzling space photo that looks like a sparkler on a dark night. The picture shows a globular cluster named NGC 6426. That's a fancy name for a giant ball of stars, all held together by gravity. Imagine 150 of these star-cities floating around our Milky Way galaxy. NGC 6426 is way out in the galaxy's halo, the outer edge. And get this: it's ancient! The stars in this cluster are about 13 billion years old. The universe itself is 13.7 billion years old. So these stars have been around almost since the beginning of time. In the image, you can see red, white, and blue stars. The colors tell us how hot they are. Blue stars are super hot, and red stars are cooler. Scientists also found that the stars have very few heavy elements, like iron. That's because they formed when the universe was young and mostly made of simple stuff like hydrogen and helium. Later, bigger stars exploded and spread heavier elements around. The cluster even has two different groups of stars: one older and one a bit younger, made from the leftovers of those explosions. Hubble took this picture to help astronomers figure out how old these clusters are and how our galaxy formed. For over 30 years, Hubble has been showing us the universe's secrets. And soon, new telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will join the party, revealing even more cosmic wonders!
why_it_matters: Learning about the universe's history helps us understand how our own planet and life came to be; the elements in our bodies were once created inside stars like these.

keywords.explanation: A tightly packed group of thousands of old stars, all held together by gravity.
The outer, round region of a galaxy, far from the center.
Elements heavier than hydrogen and helium, like iron or carbon, made inside stars.
The simplest and lightest element; the main gas in the universe.
A light gas; the second most common element in the universe.
Scientists who study stars, planets, and space.

questions.question: What is NGC 6426?
options: A. A planet.
B. A globular cluster (a giant ball of stars).
C. A new telescope.
D. A type of firework.
questions.correct_answer: B. A globular cluster (a giant ball of stars).

questions.question: How old are the stars in NGC 6426?
options: A. About 1 million years old.
B. About 13 billion years old.
C. Only a few thousand years old.
D. No one knows.

questions.question: What do the colors of the stars in the image tell us?
options: A. What country they are from.
B. How far away they are.
C. How hot they are (blue is hot, red is cooler).
D. How old they are exactly.
questions.correct_answer: C. How hot they are (blue is hot, red is cooler).

questions.question: Why do the stars have very few heavy elements like iron?
options: A. Because they are too far away.
B. Because they formed when the universe was young and mostly made of simple stuff like hydrogen and helium.
C. Because they melted them.
D. Because the telescope can't see them.
questions.correct_answer: B. Because they formed when the universe was young and mostly made of simple stuff like hydrogen and helium.

questions.question: What did Hubble's image reveal about the cluster's stars?
options: A. They are all exactly the same age.
B. They are all red.
C. There are two different groups: one older and one a bit younger, made from leftovers of earlier star explosions.
D. They are made of chocolate.
questions.correct_answer: C. There are two different groups: one older and one a bit younger, made from leftovers of earlier star explosions.

questions.question: Which future telescope will join Hubble to reveal more cosmic wonders?
options: A. James Webb Space Telescope.
B. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
C. The SpaceX Starship.
D. The Lunar Telescope.
questions.correct_answer: B. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

background_read: Globular clusters are like fossil star cities that orbit the center of galaxies like our Milky Way.
NGC 6426 is one of about 150 such clusters, containing some of the oldest known stars.

By studying them, astronomers learn what the universe was like billions of years ago, and upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (named after a pioneering NASA astronomer) will explore even more.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope and astronomers
WHAT: Captured a new image of the ancient globular cluster NGC 6426, looking like a sparkler with red, white, and blue stars
WHERE: In the outer halo of our Milky Way galaxy
WHY: To learn about the age of stars, how galaxies formed, and the history of the universe

perspectives.description: Hubble's stunning image reminds us of the beauty and mystery of space, inspiring kids to wonder about the universe.
Focusing on such distant objects can seem like a waste of time and money when there are problems on Earth.
This cluster is a natural laboratory that allows astronomers to test theories about how stars age and how galaxies formed.
